1.title: Identity Life Cycle Management
1.text: Welcome to Module seven: Identity Life Cycle Management. It covers the exam area three. Identity and Access Management. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. three point one Understand identity life cycle management: Roles definition. Provision. Review. Deprovision. Frameworks and tools. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: three. Identity and Access Management (I A M) Concepts (twenty percent). Exam format: an adaptive exam of one hundred to one hundred twenty-five questions in two hours; a score of seven hundred on a scale of one to one thousand passes. Validated against: the official I S C two C C exam outline.

1.title: The identity life cycle
1.text: The identity life cycle. An identity is the digital representation of a person, device, application or service. The life cycle follows it from creation to removal.

1.title: The identity life cycle, continued
1.text: The identity life cycle. The figure shows this: The identity life cycle: define roles, provision, review, deprovision.

1.title: The identity life cycle, continued
1.text: The identity life cycle. one Roles definition. What happens: Decide which roles exist and which access each role needs. Why it matters: Access follows the job, not the person. two Provision. What happens: Create the account and grant the role's access when someone joins. Why it matters: Right access on day one, approved by the owner. three Review. What happens: Check periodically that access is still needed (an access review or recertification). Why it matters: Stops privilege creep.

1.title: The identity life cycle, continued
1.text: The identity life cycle. four Deprovision. What happens: Disable and remove accounts and access when someone leaves or no longer needs it. Why it matters: Closes the door on former staff. The cycle is often called joiner, mover, leaver: a mover gets new access and loses the old access. Exam tip: Roles first, then provision, review, deprovision. Disable accounts at once when someone leaves, and record who approved each grant.

1.title: Privilege creep and orphaned accounts
1.text: Privilege creep and orphaned accounts. Privilege creep. Meaning: A person collects permissions over the years as they change jobs. Fix: Access reviews and removing old rights when someone moves. Orphaned account. Meaning: An account with no active owner (the owner left). Fix: Deprovision at departure; find them by reviews. Dormant account. Meaning: An account that is not used. Fix: Disable after a set period. Shared account. Meaning: Several people use one login. Fix: Avoid: actions cannot be tied to a person. Exam tip: Privilege creep is cured by access reviews and by removing the old rights when a person moves. Disable first, delete later, so that records stay for audit.

1.title: Nonhuman identities, including AI
1.text: Nonhuman identities, including A I. Service accounts, applications, devices and A I bots are identities too. They need the same life cycle. Roles definition. Define what it may do (least privilege). Provision. Create it with an owner and store secrets safely. Review. Check that it is still needed and that its rights are minimal. Deprovision. Remove it and rotate its keys when the system is retired. Exam tip: Every identity needs an owner, including bots. An A I bot with broad rights and no owner is an orphaned, over-privileged identity.

1.title: Frameworks and tools
1.text: Frameworks and tools. Identity and access management (I A M). The overall discipline and tools that manage identities and access. Directory service (for example L D A P (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), Active Directory). Central store of identities and groups. Single sign-on. One login for many applications. Federation (sam el, Open I D Connect, oh auth). Trust between organizations, so identities are reused across them. Identity governance and administration (I G A). Automates provisioning, access requests and reviews. Privileged access management (P A M). Controls and records the use of powerful accounts. Multi-factor authentication. Stronger proof of identity. Tie the system to H R: a hire, move or exit event in the H R system should trigger provisioning or deprovisioning automatically.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. An employee leaves the company. What is the best first step for the access of this person? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Disable the accounts and access at once. Deprovisioning must happen promptly so that former staff cannot keep access.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. A person has worked in four departments and still has the permissions of all four. What is this problem called? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Privilege creep from accumulated permissions. Accumulated permissions over time are privilege creep; access reviews and removal at job moves fix it.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Managers are asked every quarter to confirm that their team members still need their access. What is this process? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Access review, also called recertification. Periodic confirmation that access is still needed is an access review.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Which stage of the identity life cycle decides what access a job needs before any account is created? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Roles definition, which sets the access of a role. Roles definition comes first and describes the access each role needs.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. An A I bot that reads customer files still runs after the project that created it ended, and no one owns it. What is the best description? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: An orphaned, nonhuman identity that should be removed. Bots and service accounts are identities that need an owner and a life cycle; this one should be deprovisioned.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A company wants new staff accounts to be created automatically when H R records a hire. Which tool category supports this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Identity governance and administration. Identity governance and administration automates provisioning, requests and reviews based on H R events.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Name the four stages of the identity life cycle. Answer: Roles definition, provision, review, deprovision. Question two. What is privilege creep? Answer: Accumulating permissions over time as roles change. Question three. What does a mover need? Answer: New access and removal of the old access.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What is an orphaned account? Answer: An account with no active owner. Question five. What does S S O provide? Answer: One login for many applications. Question six. Do bots need a life cycle? Answer: Yes, like human users: owner, least privilege, review, removal.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Life cycle: roles definition, provision, review, deprovision. Joiner, mover, leaver: grant on hire, swap on move, remove on exit. Problems: privilege creep, orphaned, dormant, shared accounts. Nonhuman: bots and service accounts need owners and review. Tools: I A M, directory, S S O, federation, I G A, P A M, M F A.
